nodes.summary: If $L$ is a list of length $\ell$ with no repeated entries and $x$ is an entry of $L$, then the access cost of $x$ in $L$ plus the access cost of $x$ in the reverse of $L$ equals $\ell + 1$: the positions of $x$ in $L$ and in its reverse, counting from $1$, add up to $\ell + 1$.
nodes.title: Positions in a list and in its reverse

nodes.summary: The cost of accessing an item $x$ in a list $L$ is its position in $L$, counting from $1$: one more than the index of the first occurrence of $x$ in $L$. If $x$ does not occur in $L$, the cost is the length of $L$ plus one.
nodes.title: Access cost

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a nonempty list of $\ell$ distinct items, let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$, let $d$ be an item and $n$ a natural number, and let $\sigma$ be the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests against $A$ from its initial state, with default item $d$. Then the cost of $A$ on $\sigma$ from its initial state is $n \ell$, and there are lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, each a…
nodes.title: Online and offline costs on the adversary's sequence

nodes.summary: Given a deterministic online list-update algorithm $A$, a default item $d$, a number $n$ and a state $q$ of $A$, the adversary's sequence is the sequence of $n$ requests that starts in state $q$, always requests the last item of $A$'s current list, and then moves $A$ to its next state on that request. If the current list is empty, the default item $d$ is requested instead.
nodes.title: The list-update adversary

nodes.summary: If $L$ is a list with no repeated entries and $x$ is an entry of $L$, then the number of entries of $L$ whose index is less than the index of $x$ equals the index of $x$ (indices counted from $0$).
nodes.title: Counting the entries before an entry

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a nonempty list of $\ell$ distinct items and let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$. For every default item $d$, every natural number $n$ and every state $q$ of $A$, the cost of $A$ from state $q$ on the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests from $q$ with default item $d$ is $n \ell$.
nodes.title: The adversary makes every access cost the full length of the list

nodes.summary: The cost of a deterministic online list-update algorithm $A$ on a request sequence $x_1, \dots, x_m$ from a state $q_0$ is $c_1 + \dots + c_m$, where $q_i$ is the state $A$ moves to from $q_{i-1}$ on request $x_i$ and $c_i$ is the access cost of $x_i$ in the list of state $q_{i-1}$. The empty sequence costs $0$.
nodes.title: Cost of an online list-update algorithm

nodes.summary: A deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of `M`: a state machine whose list is always a rearrangement of `M`. Its rearrangements are free, which only strengthens the lower bound.
nodes.title: Deterministic online list-update algorithm

nodes.summary: If $x$ is an item of a list $L$, then for every index $j$ (counting from $0$), the list obtained from $L$ by the free move of $x$ to index $j$ is a rearrangement (permutation) of $L$.
nodes.title: A free move rearranges the list

nodes.summary: A free exchange (Sleator and Tarjan): right after accessing $x$ in a list $L$, move $x$ forward to index $j$ (indices counted from $0$), at no charge. If the index of $x$ in $L$ is at most $j$, the list is unchanged, so $x$ never moves backward for free; otherwise the result is obtained by erasing the first occurrence of $x$ from $L$ and inserting $x$ back so that it has index $j$.
nodes.title: Free move

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list with no repeated entries and let $a \ne x$ be entries of $M$. After erasing $x$ from $M$, the index of $a$ is unchanged if $a$ comes before $x$ in $M$, and is one less if $a$ comes after $x$ (indices counted from $0$).
nodes.title: Indices after erasing an entry

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list without duplicates, $x$ an item of $M$, and let $M'$ be the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front. For any items $a \ne x$ and $b \ne x$ of $M$, $a$ comes before $b$ in $M'$ if and only if $a$ comes before $b$ in $M$.
nodes.title: Move-to-front keeps the relative order of the other items

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list without duplicates, $x$ an item of $L$, and $N$ a list that is empty or starts with $x$, all of whose items occur in $L$. For every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $L'$ be the list obtained from $L$ by moving $x$ forward for free so that exactly $j$ items precede it, where $L' = L$ if at most $j$ items already precede $x$ in $L$. Then the number of inversions of $L'$ against $N$ is at most the number of…
nodes.title: Free moves never add inversions against a list headed by the moved item

nodes.summary: For any lists $M$ and $L$, the number of inversions of $L$ against $M$ is at most $\ell^2$, where $\ell$ is the length of $M$.
nodes.title: Inversions are at most the squared length

nodes.summary: For lists $M$ and $L$, the inversion set is the set of pairs $(a, b)$ of items of $M$ with $a$ before $b$ in $M$ and $b$ before $a$ in $L$, that is, the pairs that $M$ and $L$ order differently. Here the position of an item in a list is the index of its first occurrence, and an item that does not occur in the list sits at the position equal to the length of the list.
nodes.title: Inversion set of two lists

nodes.summary: Let $M$, $L$ and $L'$ be lists with $L$ a rearrangement of $M$. Then the number of inversions of $L'$ against $M$ is at most the number of inversions of $L$ against $M$ plus the number of inversions of $L'$ against $L$.
nodes.title: Triangle inequality for inversions

nodes.summary: For lists $M$ and $L$, the number of inversions of $L$ against $M$ is the size of their inversion set: the number of pairs $(a, b)$ of items of $M$ with $a$ before $b$ in $M$ and $b$ before $a$ in $L$, where the position of an item in a list is the index of its first occurrence, or the length of the list if it does not occur.
nodes.title: Number of inversions between two lists

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of a nonempty list $M$. Then in every state of $A$, the list of $A$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: The list of an algorithm on a nonempty list is never empty

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $L$ be lists. If a pair $(a, b)$ belongs to the inversion set of $M$ and $L$, then $a$ and $b$ are items of $M$, $a$ comes before $b$ in $M$, and $b$ comes before $a$ in $L$. Here the position of an item in a list is the index of its first occurrence, and an item that does not occur in the list sits at the position equal to the length of the list.
nodes.title: Members of the inversion set

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list without duplicates, $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$, $L_0, L_1, \dots$ lists that are each a rearrangement of $M$, and $J_0, J_1, \dots$ natural numbers. Accessing the item at position $i$ of a list, counting from $1$, costs $i$. Let $C$ be the total access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, $F$ the list it ends with, and $D$ the cost on $\sigma$ of the…
nodes.title: Amortized bound for move-to-front over a request sequence, with free exchanges

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list without duplicates, $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$, and $L_0, L_1, \dots$ lists that are each a rearrangement of $M$. Accessing the item at position $i$ of a list, counting from $1$, costs $i$. Let $C$ be the total access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, $F$ the list it ends with, and $D$ the cost on $\sigma$ of the offline algorithm without free…
nodes.title: Amortized bound for move-to-front over a request sequence

nodes.summary: In the model of Sleator and Tarjan (1985) with free exchanges, let $M$ be a list of distinct items and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$. Consider an offline algorithm given by lists $L_0, L_1, \ldots$, each a rearrangement of $M$ with $L_0 = M$, and natural numbers $J_0, J_1, \ldots$. It serves request $t$ (counting from $0$) with the list $L_t$ and pays the position of the request in $L_t$…
nodes.title: Move-to-front is 2-competitive

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list of distinct items, $L$ a rearrangement of $M$, and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$. Then the access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, plus $m$, is at most twice the cost of serving $\sigma$ with the fixed list $L$ (the sum over the requests of their positions in $L$, counting from $1$), plus the number of inversions between $M$ and $L$ (the pairs of…
nodes.title: Move-to-front against a static list

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list of distinct items and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$. Consider an offline algorithm that serves request $t$ with a list $L_t$, where every $L_t$ is a rearrangement of $M$ and $L_0 = M$: it pays the position of the request in $L_t$ (counting from $1$), and then one for each pair of items whose relative order differs between $L_t$ and $L_{t+1}$. Then the access cost of…
nodes.title: Move-to-front is 2-competitive without free exchanges

nodes.summary: Starting from a list $L$, move-to-front serves a request sequence $\sigma$ one request at a time: a request $x$ costs the position of $x$ in the current list, counting from $1$ (an item not in the list costs its length plus one), and then $x$ is moved to the front (inserted at the front if absent). The cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is the sum of these access costs.
nodes.title: Cost of move-to-front

nodes.summary: Starting from a list $L$ and serving a request sequence $\sigma$, move-to-front moves each request $x$ in turn to the front of the current list (inserting it at the front if it is absent). The final list of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is the list it ends with.
nodes.title: Final list of move-to-front

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list and $\sigma$ a request sequence whose requests are all items of $M$. From any state of online move-to-front on $M$, its access cost on $\sigma$ equals the cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from the list of that state.
nodes.title: Online move-to-front pays the move-to-front cost

nodes.summary: For a list $M$, online move-to-front is the online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$ whose states are the rearrangements of $M$, starting from $M$ itself: on a request $x$ that is in the current list it moves $x$ to the front, and it ignores requests that are not in the current list.
nodes.title: Online move-to-front

nodes.summary: If $x$ is an item of a list $M$, then the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front is a rearrangement (permutation) of $M$.
nodes.title: Move-to-front rearranges the list

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list of distinct items, $L$ a rearrangement of $M$ (the offline list), and $x$ an item of $M$ at position $k$ in $M$ and position $i$ in $L$, counting from $1$. Let $\Phi$ be the number of inversions between $M$ and $L$ (the pairs of items that the two lists order differently), and $\Phi'$ the number of inversions between the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front and $L$. Then…
nodes.title: The amortized cost of a move-to-front step

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ and an item $x$, moving $x$ to the front gives the list consisting of $x$ followed by $L$ with its first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur in $L$, this is $x$ followed by $L$.
nodes.title: Move-to-front

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a nonempty list of $\ell$ distinct items and let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$. Let $c$, $d$ and $b$ be natural numbers with $c (\ell + 1) < 2 \ell d$ (so $d \ge 1$ and $c / d < 2\ell / (\ell + 1) = 2 - 2/(\ell + 1)$). Then there are a request sequence $\sigma$, each request an item of $M$, and lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, each a rearrangement of $M$, with…
nodes.title: No deterministic online list-update algorithm beats $2 - 2/(\ell + 1)$

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ and every request sequence $\sigma$, the offline cost (without free exchanges) of serving $\sigma$ with the constant sequence of lists $L, L, L, \dots$ equals the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $L$.
nodes.title: The static cost is the offline cost of a constant list

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a natural number and let $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$ be lists, each of length at most $K$. Take every free-exchange target to be $K$; this moves nothing, since every item already has index at most $K$. Then for every request sequence $\sigma$, the offline cost with free exchanges of serving $\sigma$ with $L_0, L_1, \dots$ equals the offline cost without free exchanges of serving $\sigma$ with $L_0, L_1, \dots$.
nodes.title: Without free moves the two offline costs agree

nodes.summary: Given lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, target indices $J_0, J_1, J_2, \dots$ and a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$, let $L_t'$ be the list obtained from $L_t$ by the free exchange that moves $x_t$ forward to index $J_t$ (counting from $0$); it equals $L_t$ if $x_t$ already has index at most $J_t$. The offline cost with free exchanges of $\sigma$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in…
nodes.title: Offline cost with free exchanges

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a list of length $\ell$ and $R$ a list, and write $\mathrm{inv}(M, R)$ for the number of inversions between $M$ and $R$. For every request sequence $\sigma$ of items of $M$, the offline cost (without free exchanges) of serving $\sigma$ with the lists $M, R, R, R, \dots$ is at most $\ell + \mathrm{inv}(M, R)$ plus the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $R$.
nodes.title: Switching lists after the first request

nodes.summary: Given lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, the offline cost of a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in $L_t$ (its position, counting from $1$) plus the number of inversions between $L_t$ and $L_{t+1}$. That is, the algorithm serves request $t$ with $L_t$ and then rearranges it into $L_{t+1}$, paying one for each pair of items whose relative order it…
nodes.title: Offline cost without free exchanges

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of $\ell$ distinct items. For every request sequence $\sigma$ of $m$ items of $L$, the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $L$ plus the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with the reverse of $L$ equals $m(\ell + 1)$.
nodes.title: A list or its reverse serves any sequence at average cost at most $(\ell + 1)/2$

nodes.summary: The static cost of serving a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$ with a fixed list $L$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in $L$, its position in $L$ counting from $1$.
nodes.title: Static cost

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
